item.title: Washington Crossing the Delaware
item.museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
item.lesson: America's most famous history painting was made in Düsseldorf, Germany, by a German-American who intended it partly as a pep talk for Europe: Leutze began it amid the failed revolutions of 1848, holding up Washington's desperate Christmas-night 1776 crossing — to surprise the Hessians at Trenton — as proof that republican daring could win. Almost every detail is wrong, gloriously: the flag shown wasn't adopted until six months later; the crossing happened in darkness, not dawn; the boats were larger; and no general would stand like that in an ice-choked river. None of it matters. Leutze understood that nations run on images, and he built one at the scale of a cinema screen — over twelve by twenty-one feet — with Washington as fixed as a mast while ordinary men (farmer, frontiersman, a Black oarsman, a figure in a Scottish bonnet) strain at the oars: the idea being that everyone rows the republic. The first version was damaged by fire and later destroyed in WWII bombing; this, the second, became the icon.
item.lookFor: Study the crew instead of the general: thirteen men fill the boat — one for each colony, by most counts — and each is a different American type. The painting is a census disguised as an adventure.
